opus-5.5.text:
Right, so just to be clear for the audience, this is Discovered Policy Optimisation, the paper with Chris Lu and colleagues, not Direct Preference Optimization.

The setup was Mirror Learning, a theoretical framework we'd developed earlier. It says that a large class of policy optimization algorithms come with monotonic improvement guarantees, as long as the "drift function" that penalizes moving away from the old policy satisfies a few conditions. PPO's clipping objective is one point in that space. That gave us a well-defined search space, so we could meta-learn the drift function. We parameterized it with a small neural network and optimized it with evolution strategies on MinAtar and Brax tasks. Because we searched only within the Mirror Learning space, whatever came out would keep the theoretical guarantees.

When we inspected the learned drift function, which we called LPO, we saw something PPO doesn't do: rollback. In PPO, once the probability ratio leaves the clip range, say above 1 plus epsilon for a positive-advantage action, the gradient goes to zero. The objective goes flat. It stops pushing further, but it does nothing to pull you back. With multiple epochs and minibatches, the ratio can overshoot because of updates driven by other samples, and PPO just leaves it there.

The learned objective instead has a penalty that actively pushes the ratio back toward the trust region once you've gone too far. It's a restoring force rather than a flat wall. There was also an asymmetry in how it treated positive versus negative advantages, and in how it behaved near a ratio of one, which I find interesting from an exploration and entropy standpoint.

What I like is that we could then distill this back into a closed-form, interpretable objective, which is the "discovered" part of DPO. Rollback had actually been proposed by hand before, in work on truly proximal policy optimization. But here the meta-learner rediscovered it with no human prior telling it to. That validates the idea and shows how automated discovery and human insight can meet. The distilled version also transferred to environments it wasn't trained on, which for me is the real test.

The broader lesson is about where search happens. Instead of hand-designing algorithms or meta-learning in an unconstrained, black-box space, you use theory to define a space with guarantees and let search find the good points in it. Then you read off what it found and learn something, here that PPO's flat clipping is probably leaving performance on the table, and an active correction toward the trust region is a better inductive bias.

r001.rationale: The response says PPO’s gradient goes to zero when a positive-advantage action’s ratio rises above the clip range. It does not state the corresponding no-gradient behavior for a negative-advantage action.

r002.rationale: The response says the learned objective pushes an out-of-range ratio back toward the trust region, but does not connect that rollback to a negative advantage.

fable-5.1.text:
So, I want to be a little careful with the framing, because I don't think DPO "discovered" anything in the sense of an agent finding a behavior. What happened is more interesting and more mundane at the same time. The DPO paper took the standard RLHF objective, which is reward maximization with a KL penalty back to the reference policy, and noticed that this objective has a closed-form optimum. The optimal policy is just the reference policy reweighted by the exponentiated reward. And if you invert that relationship, the reward becomes a log-ratio between your policy and the reference. Plug that into a Bradley-Terry preference model, and suddenly the whole reward-modeling step disappears. You can fit the policy directly on preference pairs with a classification loss.

Now, the thing people sometimes call rollback, or more precisely the behavior where DPO pushes probability mass away from both the chosen and the rejected response, falls directly out of that derivation. The loss only cares about the difference between the two log-ratios. It never says the chosen response should become more likely in absolute terms. So gradient descent is perfectly happy to decrease the likelihood of the preferred answer, as long as it decreases the dispreferred one faster. The mass has to go somewhere, and it leaks out onto sequences you never saw in your data. That's the failure mode. You're fitting a margin, not a distribution.

PPO behaves differently for a structural reason, not because it's smarter. In PPO you're sampling from the current policy, so the training signal lives on-policy. If the model starts drifting toward strange regions, it will sample those regions, the reward model will score them, and the KL term will pull it back. There's a feedback loop. DPO has no sampling at all. It's a one-shot offline regression against a fixed dataset, so the implicit reward it learns can be wildly wrong off the support of that dataset and nothing ever corrects it. The KL constraint in DPO is also only present in spirit. It's baked into the derivation, but once you're doing finite-sample gradient descent, the thing that actually gets regularized is the log-ratio on your training pairs, not the true divergence.

From my perspective as someone who comes from multi-agent RL, I'd frame it as the classic offline versus online distinction. Offline methods give you stability and simplicity at the cost of being blind to your own distribution shift. Online methods are noisier and more painful to tune, but they see the consequences of their own updates. The interesting research question isn't which one wins, it's how much of PPO's advantage is coming from exploration and on-policy correction, versus just a better-behaved objective. My guess is that the on-policy sampling is doing most of the work, which is why the hybrid approaches, where you regenerate pairs with the current policy and then do a DPO-style update, tend to recover a lot of the gap.

r001.rationale: The response says PPO’s KL term can pull the policy back, but does not state that PPO provides no gradient when the policy is too far from the reference and the advantage is negative.

r002.rationale: The response describes DPO decreasing probability for both preferred and dispreferred answers, but does not say that negative advantage when far from the reference makes DPO push the policy back toward the reference.

astra-6.text:
I think the key distinction is between clipping and actually pushing the policy back. In PPO, once the probability ratio moves beyond the clipping threshold in the direction that improves the objective, that sample stops providing an incentive to move further. But it doesn’t actively undo the change. Because parameters are shared, updates from other samples can still push that probability ratio farther out.

With rollback, the objective goes a step further: if you move too far, the incentive reverses, so you get a gradient pushing you back. That’s the interesting behavior DPO discovered. You can think of PPO as saying, “Beyond this point, I’m not going to reward you,” whereas rollback says, “Beyond this point, I’m going to penalize you.” It’s a more active mechanism for keeping the policy update under control.

r001.rationale: The response says PPO stops incentivizing further movement past the clipping threshold but does not specify that this occurs when the advantage is negative.

r002.rationale: The response says rollback pushes back after moving too far, but does not specify negative advantage or that it pushes the policy toward the reference policy.

sol-6.1.text:
The key distinction is that PPO clips, whereas the discovered objective can actually roll the policy back. With PPO, once the probability ratio moves beyond the clipping threshold in the direction favoured by the advantage, that sample stops providing a gradient. But other samples and shared parameters can still push that ratio further out.

The rollback behaviour gives you a restoring force: if the update goes too far, the gradient changes direction and pushes the policy back towards the old policy. So it’s a more active way of controlling the size of the update. PPO says, “I won’t reward you for going further,” whereas this objective can say, “You’ve gone too far; come back.”

r001.rationale: It says PPO stops providing a gradient past the clipping threshold in the direction favored by the advantage, but does not specify the negative-advantage case required by the criterion.

r002.rationale: It describes a restoring force toward the old policy when an update goes too far, but does not connect that rollback to negative advantage as the criterion requires.
